position: Port the backend to Go — one binary in two roles (api, worker) against the same Postgres, keeping the React front end and keeping Bunny. Do it as a strangler, worker-first, and treat the option to stop after the worker as part of the plan rather than a failure of it.
summary: The repository does not feel unmanageable because it is large — 35,131 source lines across 295 files is small. It feels unmanageable because the runtime is scattered across four places that cannot see each other: Vercel (2 crons, vercel.json), GitHub Actions (4 more, including the notification drain), PostgREST (every query, over HTTP, with a 1,000-row cap and a URL-length limit), and the app's own process memory (rate limits, lockouts, health memos). Seven of the twelve real=true scalability findings and four of the twelve deployability ones are artefacts of that scattering, not of the code. A Go port collapses it: one long-lived process owns its own scheduler, its own connection pool, its own cache, and speaks SQL. That is a genuine structural win and it retires the single highest-severity deployability finding outright. It is also a 13-engineer-month, 8-calendar-month project for two people that touches none of the 13,326 lines of React at 17% coverage, none of the fifteen documentation findings, and none of the product gaps — no Razorpay, no invoices, no WhatsApp send, no team management. Honest verdict as this position's best advocate: the port is worth roughly 1.5 engineer-months of itself (step 3, the worker), and the remaining 11.5 are a bet that a pre-revenue product with 6 orgs and 5 catalogues should spend two-thirds of a year not shipping. I argue for the whole port because the numbers support it at scale and the cutover risk is bounded at this size — but the migration path below is deliberately ordered so that the owner can stop at month 2 with 80% of the value banked, and a judge should weigh that as the strongest thing this position has to say.
architecture:
Is there more than one service worth having? No. One Go module, one binary, two deployment roles, plus the React front end unchanged.

WHY ONE BINARY. Every service boundary you could draw here cuts through a transaction. Publish touches catalogues, titles, photos, credits and notifications in one commit (app/api/admin/catalogues/[id]/publish/route.ts, and Repository.publishCatalogueContent at lib/db/repository.ts:107-115). Handover touches orgs, operators, catalogues, transfers and notifications. Split those and you own a saga and a compensating-write story for a product with 5 catalogues. At 10 weddings/month with a peak of ~300 guests on one wedding night, a single 4-vCPU box has two orders of magnitude of headroom. Anyone selling a six-service decomposition here is selling six deployment pipelines.

THE ONE BOUNDARY THAT IS REAL: api vs worker. Same binary, `-mode=worker`, second process, Postgres advisory lock so two replicas do not double-drain. The worker owns all six jobs (lib/jobs/run.ts:49-56), the notification drain, and the Bunny webhook reconciler. It buys three things a serverless request cannot have: a usage rollup with no wall-clock ceiling (today it is O(catalogues x titles) serial provider calls in one invocation with no maxDuration, verify-scalability real=true), a scheduler nothing outside the repo can disable (today four of six jobs ride a public repo's GitHub Actions, which self-disable after 60 days of no commits — the one high-severity deployability finding), and failure isolation: a crashed drain cannot take the guest page down.

THE BOUNDARY THAT IS NOT REAL: guest read vs admin write. They are the same rows. The guest path is a cache over the admin path's writes, which is exactly what lib/catalogue-cache.ts is. Splitting them means inventing a cache-invalidation protocol between two services to replace a function call. Instead: one binary, one in-process read model — a sync.Map keyed by catalogue slug, invalidated on Publish, fanned out to other replicas by Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY. That is ~200 lines and it is strictly better than revalidateTag, because you can see it and test it.

DATA LAYER. Drop PostgREST, keep Postgres (keep Supabase as the managed Postgres and as gotrue for auth; you are dropping the HTTP query layer, not the vendor). pgx + sqlc: the 24 migrations in supabase/migrations/ are already plain SQL and port verbatim. The ~20 field-to-column maps that today live as hand-written object literals (only 2 are pinned to the schema by a test, verify-maintainability real=true) become generated structs — the map cannot drift from the column because it is generated from the column. This is the honest answer to the highest-severity maintainability finding: the two-driver design already failed at its one job. lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1392 still filters listTitles on `published` and `status` and never on `live_at`, while lib/db/memory-repository.ts:747 gets it right and says so in a comment; the photo half of the same bug was patched only after the 15 Sept review (commit 7730633), whose own new comment concedes "no behavioural test runs against this driver." One implementation against the real engine makes that class of divergence structurally impossible.

WHAT PORTS. lib/db 3,868 + lib/admin 1,112 + lib/video 629 + lib/notify 590 + lib/domains 428 + lib/health 256 + lib/photos 230 + lib/http 194 + lib/auth 109 + lib/captcha 83 + lib/my 56 + lib/jobs 56 = 7,611 lines, plus ~2,200 of the 3,329 root lib lines that are server-side (schema.ts 690, catalogue-access, lifecycle, entitlements, downloads, tenant, auth, crypto, env), plus 61 API route files ≈ 4,300 lines. ~14,000 TypeScript lines of server logic → roughly 20,000–25,000 lines of Go at the usual 1.4–1.8x.

THE SEAMS PORT WELL. This codebase was already written against interfaces, and that is the main reason the port is costable at all. lib/video/provider.ts:4-7 is five methods with no provider types leaking ("switching from Bunny to Cloudflare is a new implementation of this interface and one line") — that is a Go interface verbatim. modules/registry.ts:15 is the only place a module type is named, held by a test, and it is entirely front-end so it does not move. lib/catalogue-access.ts:9-14 is 88 lines and one switch; it becomes one Go function that every handler calls. lib/env.ts's seven driver enums (:48,:64,:100,:105,:127,:161,:170) become seven constructor switches.

FRONT END: keep Next.js, do not go to Vite. All 40 pages are server components (zero carry 'use client'); 64 of 70 components and 83 of the client files are client-side already. So the Next server surface is 40 page files that fetch and compose — they keep working, their data just comes from the Go API over HTTP instead of getRepository(). A Vite SPA would mean the guest page renders as HTML → JS bundle → API call → paint, which is strictly worse for the number that defines Phase 0 done (1.5s on 4G). The admin console could move to Vite and buys nothing for it. Keep one Next app; delete lib/db from it.

MIDDLEWARE GETS SIMPLER, NOT LOST. middleware.ts is 122 lines of host/path → rewrite with a stated constraint it apologises for: "The slug is unknown until the database is consulted, which middleware must not do" (:100). That is why app/d/[host]/ exists as a whole extra route tree. In Go the router can consult the database, so /d/<host> is deleted and the custom-domain path becomes a cache lookup. 40 lines of chi.

CONTRACT. The port's specification already exists: lib/db/repository.ts is a 404-line interface with the semantics written as doc comments. Generate OpenAPI from the Go handlers, generate the TypeScript client and Zod schemas from that. This is the one new permanent piece of infrastructure the port adds, and it is the piece most likely to rot — see costs.
benefits: Retires the one high-severity deployability finding structurally, not by remembering to commit. Four of six jobs — the notification drain, the lapse ladder, expiry warnings, the synthetic check — ride a public repo's GitHub Actions, which disable themselves after 60 days without commits (.github/workflows/notify-drain.yml:14-15), and the alert about that failure is queued in the queue that stopped draining. A worker process with an internal scheduler and a Postgres advisory lock cannot be switched off by a quiet fortnight. This alone is ~1.5 engineer-months and is available in month 2 of the plan.

Kills four real=true findings that are pure PostgREST artefacts: nothing is paginated and PostgREST's default row cap truncates list reads with no error; .in() with an unbounded id array returns HTTP 414 and breaks a large studio's own console home page; the platform console does one round trip per org (N+1); catalogueCounts fetches unbounded row sets to compute numbers the Repository interface's own comment (lib/db/repository.ts:46-53) says it exists to avoid. In pgx these are one SELECT ... GROUP BY, one LIMIT/OFFSET, one = ANY($1::uuid[]). You cannot write the N+1 by accident once you have SQL.

One driver instead of two, tested against the real engine. The liveOnly/live_at divergence (high, in both verify-maintainability and verify-scalability) exists because the driver production runs on is executed by no test; lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1392 still ignores live_at for titles today. sqlc generates the mapping from the column, and a Go test against a throwaway Postgres runs the same suite the memory driver ran — the divergence has nowhere to live.

Changes the playback-heartbeat cost model by an order of magnitude. The 10-second heartbeat is ~12x the function budget SCALE-PLAN assumes and costs five Supabase round trips each (medium, real=true); play_events then accumulate forever at one row per heartbeat with a retention column nothing reads. A Go process buffers heartbeats in memory and flushes a batched COPY every 30 seconds — one write per catalogue per half-minute instead of one function invocation per guest per ten seconds.

Makes the 1.5s-on-4G budget easier rather than harder — provided the guest page stays server-rendered, which this architecture does. No cold starts, a warm pgx pool in bom1, and a bundle read from process memory rather than four round trips through PostgREST.

Per-process state stops being a lie in two of the three places it currently is. The passcode lockout and the health-probe memo assume they are global and are not (low, real=true); the rate limiter's own comment says so (lib/http/rate-limit.ts:1-12). With one api process they simply are global; with two, a Redis client in a long-lived process is trivial where it is awkward per-invocation.

Tooling covers the whole module with no configuration question. `pnpm lint` does not visit middleware.ts, modules/ or themes/, which makes `pnpm verify` greener than the codebase and breaks the first rule in CLAUDE.md's enforced table in four places (medium, real=true). go vet and staticcheck have no include list to get wrong.
A migration ledger and a CLI applier come free with goose or golang-migrate. Today schema changes reach production by pasting SQL into a web console with no ledger (medium, real=true).

Cost ceiling becomes a rented box rather than a metered invocation. At 300 weddings/month SCALE-PLAN §3 names Vercel's function-invocation ceiling as the binding limit; a Hetzner CPX31 does not have one.

Bunny is kept, which the cost model independently supports: ₹7,534/month at 10 weddings against ₹19,971 infra-only self-hosted, 7.3x dearer once people are counted (cost.json, 10-weddings scenario). This position does not spend any of its budget re-fighting that.
costs_and_losses: The hermetic test suite is the real loss and it should not be softened. 659 unit tests run today with no Docker, no database, on any laptop, in seconds, because MemoryRepository exists — and CLAUDE.md argues for exactly that at length ('a test suite that needs a database is a test suite nobody runs'). The Go replacement is standard and fast (one shared container, BEGIN/ROLLBACK per test) but it needs Docker on every dev machine and in CI, it is a new harness to build and maintain, and it fails differently on a plane. Counter-argument, which is the honest one: the memory driver already failed at its one job — driver parity — and shipped unpublished photographs to production guests.

Zod's double duty ends, and the shape is maintained twice. lib/schema.ts is 690 lines doing runtime validation AND producing the TypeScript types the entire codebase reads. Go gives you structs and a validator; the React front end still needs Zod. Unless OpenAPI generation is kept honest on every change, the two drift silently. This is the single largest recurring tax of the port and it is invisible in month 1.

Preview deployments. Vercel gives a working URL per pull request for free, which is genuinely useful for a customizer you show a studio before merging. Reproducing it means a per-branch container and a per-branch database, and nobody budgets it.

Vercel crons: a small, real loss — exactly two entries (reconcile, usage in vercel.json). The other four already live outside Vercel, so on net the port converts four fragile jobs into six real ones. Do not let anyone sell this as a large loss in either direction.

ISR: almost nothing is lost, and the honest correction matters. The guest page is NOT ISR-cached today and cannot be — lib/catalogue-cache.ts:13-16 explains that /c/[slug] declares revalidate but reads cookies() for locale, profile and passcode grant, which opts it out of static generation entirely. The capacity plan assuming otherwise is itself a real=true finding. What is actually lost is Next's DATA cache (unstable_cache + revalidateTag): free, disk-backed under .next/cache, surviving deploys, with tag invalidation. Rebuilding it in Go is a week (sync.Map + LISTEN/NOTIFY), and the result is inspectable — but it is a week that is free today.

A staging environment becomes your problem, and you did not have one before (medium, real=true: 'a migration and the build that needs it meet for the first time in production'). The port does not fix this; it makes not fixing it more dangerous, because you now also own the runtime.

Infra cost goes UP at current scale, not down. Today: Vercel Pro + Supabase Pro ≈ ₹4,100/month plus Bunny ₹7,534 ≈ ₹11,650. After: 2x Hetzner CPX31 ≈ ₹2,800, load balancer ₹560, Supabase Pro retained for Postgres/gotrue ₹2,250, Vercel Pro for the Next front end ₹1,800, monitoring and backups ₹900, Bunny unchanged ₹7,534 ≈ ₹15,800/month. The port pays back somewhere past ~150 weddings/month, not before.

Eight calendar months during which no customer-visible feature ships unless the team deliberately splits. Razorpay (N-20, zero payment code, zero payment env vars), invoices, the empty plans table, WhatsApp send, studio team management — all of it waits, or the 13 engineer-months becomes 18.

A one-language product becomes two-language. Today one person can hold the whole thing. After, the minimum viable team is a Go person and a React person, and the rare, expensive hire is the one who can do both — which is precisely the person the front-end rewire needs.

Every one of the fifteen documentation findings becomes worse on day one. The docs are already the most stale artefact in the tree (the two files CLAUDE.md tells you to read first are the most stale documents in it; ARCHITECTURE.md, named the best single entry point in two places, predates a third of the shipped surface). A port invalidates all of them at once, and re-documenting is not in the 13 months.
what_it_does_not_fix: 13,326 lines of React across 75 files at 17% line coverage, with no component test at all on the four largest — CustomizerShell (765) and CreateWizard (1,006) among them. Every line survives the port untouched.

CreateWizard's 29 useState hooks and its 70-line create() with two sequenced network calls and inline response casts. Wizard draft persistence that mirrors only step-1 fields to localStorage. All unchanged.
Both language dictionaries shipping in the guest bundle against a budget with 4KB of headroom. Front end.

Every open security item: N-83 (photo pull zone has no token auth — any leaked URL returns 200 forever), N-85 (a passcode currently grants the full download manifest against Sandeep's own D-43 rule), N-86 (no CSP, CAPTCHA_DRIVER=none in production). These are decisions and a day of work each; the port neither helps nor hurts, except by delaying them eight months.

The entire commerce subsystem: no Razorpay, no invoice table, plans table with zero rows and no reader, catalogue-level entitlements that no route can write, 'archive' that reduces no storage while PRICING.md prices it as if it does, and a 20 GB enforced default against 100–200 GB sold.
The Bunny webhook URL that nothing in the repo can read, verify or change — the failure that already caused one real incident at the domain switchover. It is a dashboard setting; it stays one.

'The repository feels unmanageable.' Count what the Go version has: 61 handlers, 24 migrations, ~80 sqlc queries, the same 70 React components, the same 9 modules, the same 40 pages. The count does not go down. It goes up by one language and one code-generation step. If the feeling is about comprehension rather than load, a port is the wrong instrument — and at 6 orgs and 5 catalogues, the feeling is about comprehension.
risks: You are porting against a specification that is wrong in known and unknown ways. The nine subsystem maps list roughly eighty undocumented behaviours; the documentation assessment found that four price documents disagree and no price exists in code at all, that README's 'Known gaps' describes a prototype the product is a phase past, and that the advertised cold-start reading path is wrong by 5.6x. Every undocumented behaviour is a latent difference a customer finds first.

The highest-severity finding is itself proof of this risk class. The team shipped a two-driver semantic divergence (listTitles ignoring live_at) that no test could see, and only the photo half has been patched. A port is that same class of bug, two hundred times larger, arriving all at once.

Classic rewrite risk, bounded by size but not by consequence. 35k lines is not Netscape. The failure mode here is not 'never finishes' — it is 'finishes in month 8 exactly where month 0 was, minus eight months of compounding at 10 weddings/month, and minus the Razorpay integration that would have made the thing a business.'

Bunny signed-URL parity. lib/video/bunny.ts is ~330 lines of URL signing with exact semantics against a live protected zone (token auth, referrer blocking, IP pinning). Get a byte wrong and playback 403s for guests only, in production only. `pnpm preflight` exists and checks most of it, which is the mitigation — but not the webhook, and not token enforcement on the photo zone.

Resumable multi-gigabyte upload. CLAUDE.md names components/admin/UploadManager.tsx as where doc 13 §7 says the schedule slips, and instructs that the offset handling not be simplified. The client survives the port; the server that brokers the tus ticket and reconciles offsets does not, and it is the least forgiving thing to re-derive.

The E2E harness does not survive intact. 212 Playwright tests across 17 files rely on ALLOW_EPHEMERAL_DATA, the memory driver, a shared store, a demo fixture reached by slug, a registration budget, and the __catalogue query-param override (middleware.ts:64-77). All of that has to be rebuilt against a seeded Postgres before a single E2E run means anything again — and it is the only integration test the parallel workflow relies on.

Velocity is assumed from an anomalous baseline. 179 commits and ~35k lines in five weeks came from one author plus an agent. Agent assistance is weaker on a port than on greenfield, because the correctness criterion is 'matches undocumented behaviour of the old system' and the agent cannot check that. If you plan the port at greenfield velocity you will miss by 2x.

Two-language coordination cost between two people. The interface between them is generated code; if generation drifts even once during the eight months, both halves are wrong in a way types do not catch on either side.

The port's own value is concentrated in its first quarter. If the plan is executed out of order — API first, worker last — the money is spent before any of it is banked, and an abandoned port leaves a half-strangled system that is worse than either end state.
triggers_to_revisit: STOP AND SHIP INSTEAD if Razorpay and a working invoice are not live by month 3 of the port. A pre-revenue product with 6 orgs cannot fund an eight-month infrastructure project out of hope.

STOP AFTER STEP 3 (the worker, ~1.5 engineer-months) if the shadow-read in step 2 finds fewer than about three real behavioural divergences. That would mean the TypeScript codebase is more correct than the review suggests, and the remaining 11.5 engineer-months are buying ergonomics, not correctness.

STOP if the next sixty days of bug reports come predominantly from CreateWizard, CustomizerShell and the upload manager rather than from the API or the jobs. That is the front end, and the port is then treating the wrong organ — spend the months on component tests for the 13,326 untested lines instead.

STOP if the second hire is a React engineer. This architecture needs the Go half staffed by someone who has shipped Go, and a two-language stack with one language staffed is worse than a one-language stack.

ACCELERATE if monthly weddings pass ~150. Vercel function invocations, the 10-second heartbeat's five round trips, and the nightly O(catalogues x titles) rollup all become binding around there, and the rented box does not.

ACCELERATE if PostgREST's row cap or the .in() 414 actually truncates a studio's console before month 3 — that converts a low-severity finding into a customer-visible one and moves the data layer to the front of the queue.

REVISIT THE WHOLE DECISION if a second driver-parity bug is found in the TypeScript codebase before the port begins. Two is a pattern, and it makes the single-implementation argument decisive rather than merely strong.
REVISIT if Supabase or Vercel changes pricing or limits materially, in either direction — the infra arithmetic here is ₹4,200/month against the port at current scale and is not robust to a 2x move.
migration_path: Weeks 0–2 — Write the contract, change nothing. lib/db/repository.ts is already a 404-line interface with its semantics in doc comments; that is the port's specification and it exists. Introduce a third TypeScript implementation, RepositoryHttpClient, that speaks the same interface over HTTP to a Go service with zero methods implemented so far. Nothing in app/ or components/ changes. Reuse the 24 SQL migrations verbatim; stand up goose and pin the current schema as the baseline. Cost: 0.5 engineer-months.

Month 1 — Read path in Go, shadowed. Implement getCatalogueBySlug, listTitles, listPhotosForCatalogue and the guest bundle in Go with sqlc. Run it beside the live app: the Next app calls both the Supabase driver and the Go service, returns the Supabase answer, and logs any divergence. This is precisely how the live_at bug would have been caught rather than shipped, and it is the cheapest possible test of whether the port is finding real problems. Cost: 1.5 engineer-months.

Month 2 — THE WORKER, AND THE FIRST PLACE IT IS SAFE TO STOP. Move all six jobs, the notification drain and the Bunny webhook reconciler into the Go binary on an internal scheduler behind a Postgres advisory lock. Delete both GitHub Actions workflows and both vercel.json cron entries. Touches no guest-facing path, no session, no playback token. This retires the one high-severity deployability finding, uncaps the usage rollup, batches the heartbeat writes, and removes the copy-pasted non-constant-time cron bearer check from six routes. If the owner reads nothing else in this document: about 80% of the port's value is banked here, for about 1.5 of its 13 engineer-months. Cost: 1.5 engineer-months.

Months 3–5 — Admin write path, one route at a time, behind a per-route flag. 61 API routes; the admin ones first because they are behind a login and a mistake reaches one operator rather than three hundred guests. Each route's existing E2E test is its acceptance criterion, which is why the E2E harness rebuild (step 7's work, pulled forward) starts here rather than later. Port lib/admin/session.ts first and hold the org-scoping rule with a compile-time pattern, not a convention — it is the only rule in CLAUDE.md's enforced table with no automated check today. Cost: 4 engineer-months.

Month 6 — Guest read path, playback tokens and signed URLs last. The 1.5s budget and every security token live here. Port lib/catalogue-access.ts as one function; port lib/video/bunny.ts's signing and prove parity against the live protected zone with the existing preflight script extended to cover the photo zone's token enforcement and the webhook URL. Fix N-83, N-85 and N-86 in Go while you are in this code rather than twice. Cost: 2.5 engineer-months.

Month 7 — Cut lib/db out of Next. The 40 server pages keep their shape and lose getRepository() for the generated typed client; delete both drivers, including the memory driver. Stand up the Go test harness properly: one shared Postgres container, a transaction per test rolled back, the same assertions the 659 vitest cases made. Replace Next's data cache with the sync.Map + LISTEN/NOTIFY read model. Delete app/d/[host]/ — the Go router can consult the database, which is the constraint middleware.ts:100 exists to work around. Cost: 2 engineer-months.

Month 8 — Staging, pipeline, cutover. Build the staging environment you never had (this is the medium-severity finding the port does not otherwise fix). Two systemd units or a small container platform, TLS, log shipping, nightly Postgres backups with a restore drill actually performed, blue-green deploy, rollback rehearsed twice. Dual-run api and Vercel for a week with traffic split by catalogue, compare, then flip DNS. Keep the Vercel deployment warm and revertible for thirty days. Cost: 1 engineer-month, and it is the line most likely to be underestimated.
evidence: lib/db/repository.ts:29-39 — the persistence seam's own rationale, and the 404-line interface that is the port's ready-made specification.

lib/db/repository.ts:46-53 — CatalogueCounts exists specifically to avoid 'sixty round trips to draw one screen'; verify-scalability finds it now fetches unbounded row sets to do it, which is the PostgREST ceiling, not a coding mistake.
lib/db/repository.ts:339-343 — listPhotosForCatalogue declares liveOnly as the guest's view.

lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1390-1396 — listTitles filters `published` and `status`, never `live_at`. Still true in the working tree at HEAD 96fb305; the titles half of the highest-severity finding is live in production today.

lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1627-1641 — the photo half was patched only after the 15 Sept review (commit 7730633), and the patch's own comment concedes 'no behavioural test runs against this driver.'
lib/db/memory-repository.ts:747 — the memory driver gets live_at right and explains why, which is the divergence the two-driver design was supposed to prevent.

lib/catalogue-cache.ts:13-16 — 'Why not static rendering': /c/[slug] declares revalidate but reads cookies(), which opts it out of static generation entirely. The guest page is not ISR-cached, so a port loses the data cache, not ISR.

middleware.ts:100 — 'The slug is unknown until the database is consulted, which middleware must not do' — the constraint that forces the whole app/d/[host]/ route tree to exist, and which a Go router does not have.
middleware.ts:64-77 — the __catalogue query-param override gated on ALLOW_EPHEMERAL_DATA, which is how the E2E suite reaches a catalogue without a database; part of the harness a port must rebuild.
lib/catalogue-access.ts:9-14 and :30-64 — 88 lines and one ordered switch: the entire guest authorisation surface, and one of the cheapest things in the repo to port correctly.
lib/video/provider.ts:1-8 — 'Five methods, no provider types leaking past this file' — a Go interface as written, and the reason keeping Bunny costs the port nothing.
modules/registry.ts:15 — 'The ONLY place a module is wired in', held by tests/unit/registry.test.ts; entirely front-end, so all 9 modules and 2,213 lines survive the port untouched.

vercel.json — exactly two crons (reconcile, usage); the other four jobs in lib/jobs/run.ts:49-56 ride GitHub Actions, which .github/workflows/notify-drain.yml:14-15 says disable themselves after 60 days of repo inactivity.
lib/env.ts:48,64,100,105,127,161,170 — seven driver enums (data, video, notify, photo, domain, auth, captcha), each already a swap point; the port replaces implementations, not architecture.
package.json — 14 runtime dependencies, of which @supabase/ssr and @supabase/supabase-js are the two the port removes and hls.js, tus-js-client, @dnd-kit/* and lucide-react are front-end and stay.
Measured 15 Sept 2026: all 40 pages are server components (zero carry 'use client'); 64 of 70 components are client. The RSC surface a port must rewire is 40 data-loading page files, not 115.
cost.json, 10-weddings scenario — Bunny ₹7,534/month against ₹19,971 self-hosted infra-only and ₹54,971 with people, 7.3x dearer. Keeping Bunny is the settled part of this position.

docs/SCALE-PLAN.md:32-38 — Vercel Pro + Supabase Pro at ₹25,785 per six months (~₹4,300/month), infrastructure at 16.8% of revenue at 60 weddings; the baseline the port's ₹15,800/month is measured against.
verify-deployability.json — the 60-day GitHub Actions self-disable is the only high-severity deployability finding, and it is the finding this position's month-2 step retires outright.

verify-maintainability.json — 13,326 lines of UI at 17% coverage with no component test on the four largest files; CreateWizard at 1,006 lines with 29 useState hooks. None of it is touched by a backend port.
